title: Redefining student assessment in AI-infused learning environments: a systematic review of challenges and strategies for academic integrity
authors: Prince Daughin Ngqabutho Ncube; Godwin Pedzisai Dzvapatsva; Courage Matobobo; Memory M Ranga
ft_reason: HE assessment and academic integrity under GenAI is the central focus; peer-reviewed systematic review published 2025 (issue 2026), English. Meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Systematic review (PRISMA-guided) with inductive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) of included empirical studies
country: South Africa / UK (author affiliations); included studies international
discipline: Higher education generally (cross-disciplinary); includes some IT/engineering education sources
level: Higher education (undergraduate and postgraduate; not separated)
sample: Scopus (20), IEEE Xplore (300) and ScienceDirect (65) = 385 records; 382 after deduplication; 118 full texts screened; 56 empirical studies included (2015-2025 window)
assessment_types: Supervised assessment; Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Staged submissions; Process evidence; Personalised tasks; AI-use declarations
key_findings: Six themes were grouped into two categories: challenges to integrity in unsupervised assessments (AI-enabled dishonesty, over-reliance, reliability/fairness of AI-generated work) and strategies (AI-resistant/process-based assessment, institutional policy and literacy, human-AI collaboration). [Sec 3.5 p.5; Sec 4 p.6; Tables 2-4 p.7] | Included studies report that conventional plagiarism tools such as Turnitin are unreliable for AI-generated text (false positives and negatives), and many institutions lack clear AI-in-assessment guidelines, leaving staff inconsistent. [Sec 4.1.1 p.7-8; Sec 4.1.3 p.8] | The literature favours oral exams/vivas, scaffolded multi-stage submissions with drafts, reflective journals, higher-order Bloom tasks and real-world problem tasks as AI-resistant, process-focused designs. [Sec 4.2.1 p.8-9] | Some universities have introduced mandatory AI-disclosure requirements and AI-literacy programmes for students and staff to promote transparency and responsible use. [Sec 4.2.2 p.9] | AI-assisted assessment may widen inequity, since students with better access to AI tools gain an advantage. [Sec 4.1.3 p.8]
author_recommendations: Use oral vivas routinely as part of assessment, not only to verify authenticity when misconduct is alleged (not tested) | Add sections to rubrics where students declare how they used AI (not tested) | Assess throughout the learning process (process-oriented, multi-stage assessment) rather than only the final product (not tested) | Specify which AI platforms may be used, choosing ones all learners can access, to support equity (not tested) | Institutions should adopt AI policy frameworks and provide AI-literacy and assessment-design professional development for staff (not tested)
limitations: Authors note over-reliance on literature dominated by educator voices (p.11). Other issues: only three databases; the search string required the phrase 'Academic Integrity'; no formal quality appraisal of included studies; 2015-2025 window extends before GenAI; results are not split by discipline or level.
quality_note: Clear RQ and transparent PRISMA flow with numbers. However, there was no critical appraisal of included studies, and the narrow search string and three databases limit how comprehensive it is.
dim_authenticity: Recommends authentic, application-based tasks (e.g., real-life problem-solving projects) as both more valid and harder to outsource to AI.
dim_capability_verification: Proposes routine oral vivas, rather than only after suspected misconduct, to confirm that students understand their own work.
dim_integrity_security: Synthesises evidence that AI detectors are unreliable and that unsupervised essays and take-home assignments are especially vulnerable.
dim_lo_alignment: Argues assessments should target higher-order Bloom levels (create/evaluate) that current GenAI handles less well.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Advocates AI-use declarations in rubrics, human-AI collaboration, and critique of AI outputs rather than outright bans.
dim_workload: Notes that AI-based grading promises efficiency but has reliability and fairness limits.
dim_feasibility: Mentions supervised, time-constrained assessment as a fallback but notes criticism that it is distant from real-world tasks.
dim_process_visibility: Multi-stage submissions with drafts let educators follow learning progress and students' interaction with AI over time.
dim_accessibility_equity: Flags the digital divide and unequal access to AI tools; suggests naming AI platforms that all learners can access.

title: A scoping review on how generative artificial intelligence transforms assessment in higher education
authors: Qi Xia; Xiaojing Weng; Fan Ouyang; Tzung‐Jin Lin; Thomas K. F. Chiu
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
ft_reason: HE context; assessment transformation and academic integrity under GenAI is the primary focus; peer-reviewed scoping review (2024, English).
study_design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of empirical studies; ERIC, Web of Science, Scopus; search completed 30 Sep 2023
country: Hong Kong/China and Taiwan (authors); reviewed studies from 18 regions
discipline: Multi-disciplinary (education, medicine and computer science most common among 11 disciplines)
sample: 969 records retrieved; 32 empirical studies included
assessment_types: Supervised assessment; Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Practical demonstrations; Personalised tasks; AI-use declarations
key_findings: Of the 27 articles addressing students, 54% flagged GenAI as a significant challenge to academic integrity, with evidence that ChatGPT can pass exams and achieve high grades on short-form essays. [p. 7, Sec 'Student academic integrity'] | Reviewed studies called for more diverse and innovative assessment; presentations and live or pre-recorded discussions were rated least affected by ChatGPT, and video-conference questioning was proposed as an alternative. [pp. 8-9, Sec 'More diverse and innovative assessment'] | Short-term mitigations reported in the literature include oral presentations, in-person exams, projects and laboratory work, since face-to-face knowledge-based assessment was seen as not threatened by ChatGPT. [p. 13, Sec 'Disrupting traditional assessment methods'] | At teacher level, the review identifies needs for assessment and AI literacy and a balanced, mixed human/AI assessment approach in which teachers assess ideas and reasoning that GenAI cannot. [pp. 7-10, Fig. 4; Sec 'Balancing GenAI and human assessment'] | At institution level, assessment policies need redesign, including clear GenAI usage rules; transparent disclosure of tool use may mean use is not treated as plagiarism. [p. 11, Sec 'Redesigning assessment policies'; Fig. 5]
author_recommendations: Provide teacher professional development on assessment, AI and digital literacy (not tested). | Strengthen teacher beliefs about combining human and AI assessment, moving to mixed methods (not tested). | Institutions should review assessment policies, diversify assessment beyond exams and essays, and offer more interdisciplinary programmes (not tested). | Future research on discipline-tailored assessment strategies and standardised assessment policy (not tested).
limitations: Authors note that, as a scoping review, it cannot give specific recommendations and that many included studies discussed GenAI generically without naming technologies (p. 17). Most included studies date from 2023; there was a single search date (30 Sep 2023) and no quality appraisal of the included studies is reported.
quality_note: Clear RQs, PRISMA-ScR process with dual coding and a coding table; limitations stated briefly. Synthesis is descriptive and percentages are based on small counts.
dim_authenticity: Reports calls for authentic, higher-order and case-based tasks that are hard for AI to replicate (pp. 9-10).
dim_capability_verification: Reports that ChatGPT passes many exams and essays, undermining traditional tasks as evidence of student learning (p. 7, p. 13).
dim_integrity_security: Integrity is the main student-level challenge (54% of articles); in-person and oral formats are proposed as more secure (pp. 7, 13).
dim_lo_alignment: Argues critical thinking, problem solving, creativity and AI/digital literacy should be explicit learning outcomes and assessed (p. 9, p. 14).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Recommends balancing AI-assisted and human assessment and clear institutional rules on GenAI use (pp. 10-11).
dim_workload: Notes assessment was historically manual and time-intensive and that GenAI may provide immediate feedback (pp. 2, 5-6); no workload data.
dim_feasibility: Calls for teacher professional development in assessment and AI literacy as a precondition for change (p. 14).
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes possible bias in GenAI feedback and the need for equitable AI access (pp. 2, 6).

title: Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education
authors: Nadeera Ahangama
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
ft_reason: HE ICT programmes (AQF 7-9, Australia); assessment redesign for GenAI is the primary focus; peer-reviewed framework paper, 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Qualitative interpretivist web-based document analysis with Braun & Clarke six-phase thematic analysis, used to build a conceptual framework (GENESIS) and an Assessment Design Matrix (ADM)
discipline: ICT / computing (cybersecurity, software development, data analytics, information systems, ML)
sample: 80 publicly available English-language web documents (journal articles, university policies/procedures, practice and concept papers, 2023-2025), found by Google searches on 5-9 March 2025; 185 initial codes; saturation reported at 72 documents
assessment_types: Supervised assessment; Oral assessments; Practical demonstrations; Staged submissions; Process evidence; Personalised tasks
key_findings: The thematic analysis produced 7 key themes and 70 subthemes. The author argues they form a sequence for institution-wide reform: values, governance, support infrastructure, AI-integrated curriculum, then graduate competencies, strategies and methods. [p. 6 (Results); Table 1, pp. 7-8; Fig. 1] | 18 assessment strategies were identified. They include in-person assessment of foundational knowledge, multi-staged connected scaffolding, assessing process over product, personalised authentic contexts, GenAI de-scaffolding, pre-testing tasks with GenAI, and invigilated gatekeeping assessments. [Theme 6, pp. 17-20; Table 1] | 19 assessment methods were listed. Examples are process documentation with iterative evidence, debugging/code-tracing tasks, hackathons, controlled exams, interviews/presentations/demonstrations with Q&A to check authenticity, milestone group projects and multi-stage essays. [Theme 7, pp. 20-21; Table 1, p. 8] | Securing every task was described as unrealistic. Instead, programmes should identify key stage-gate assessments (e.g. capstones, demonstrations) for heightened security, and use assessment triangulation across the degree. [Theme 4 (AC4, AC5), pp. 14-15] | Detection tools raised concerns about false positives, bias and fairness, including for non-native English speakers. The sources favour process-oriented, in-person evidence collection over detection. [Theme 1 (VD2) p. 8; Theme 2 (G3) p. 10]
author_recommendations: Adopt the five-pillar GENESIS framework as an institution-wide approach to assessment reform, starting from values and governance (not tested) | Use the Assessment Design Matrix: select at least one graduate competency, strategy and method per assessment and verify the alignment (not tested) | Secure key gatekeeping assessments (e.g. capstones, core technical units) through supervision/invigilation rather than securing every task (not tested) | Pre-test assessment tasks with GenAI before release (not tested) | Empirically validate GENESIS/ADM through pilots, educator/student feedback and longitudinal mixed-methods studies
limitations: Author-stated: the derived lists are limited to what the analysed documents covered; data were limited to public, English-language web documents from a short period, which may not reflect internal practice or tacit knowledge; the frameworks have not been empirically validated (p. 36). Reviewer note: single analyst with no reported second coder; the documents were selected by Google search-result order.
quality_note: Clear RQ; transparent document-analysis/TA procedure with dates, search strings and an 80-document appendix; themes are backed by source excerpts; limitations stated. Caveats: single coder, and the frameworks are unvalidated.
dim_authenticity: Recommends personalised, authentic-context and real-life problem-solving tasks, mapped to ICT graduate competencies (AS9, AM12, AM16; pp. 19-21).
dim_capability_verification: Proposes in-person assessment of foundational ICT knowledge and Q&A in interviews and demonstrations to verify depth of understanding (AS1, AM15; pp. 17, 21).
dim_integrity_security: Proposes securing selected gatekeeping assessments through supervision/invigilation rather than every task, and moving away from reliance on detection (AC4, AS18, G3; pp. 10, 14, 20).
dim_lo_alignment: The ADM links graduate competencies, strategies and methods, and the author maps it to constructive alignment and evidence-centred design (pp. 26-34; Table 3).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Calls for institutions to quantify the AI use allowed for each assessment type and to treat GenAI literacy and prompt engineering as graduate attributes (G2, AC3, GC1, GC8; pp. 9, 14-17).
dim_scalability: Claims the ADM can be scaled and adapted to other disciplines by changing graduate attributes, but this has not been empirically tested (p. 36).
dim_workload: Notes the need to recalibrate assessment volume as staged and supervised tasks grow, and lists workload pressure as an implementation challenge (AC2, p. 13; p. 36).
dim_feasibility: Names staff resistance, resource limits and workload as practical barriers to implementation (p. 36).
dim_process_visibility: Recommends process-over-product assessment using prompts, reflective commentaries, planning notes and time-stamped drafts (AS7, AM1; pp. 18, 20).
dim_accessibility_equity: Highlights equitable access to GenAI tools, detector bias against non-native speakers, and challenges for neurodivergent and socially anxious students with new formats such as in-class Q&A (G5, SI3, SI5; pp. 10-12).

title: Assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
authors: Zachari Swiecki; Hassan Khosravi; Guanliang Chen; Roberto Martínez‐Maldonado; Jason M. Lodge; Sandra Milligan; Neil Selwyn; Dragan Gašević
ft_reason: Amendment 3 (redesign focus): Pre-GenAI review of AI-enabled assessment systems
study_design: Conceptual/critical narrative review (explicitly non-exhaustive, footnote 2)
country: Australia (author affiliations: Monash, Queensland, Melbourne); setting not country-specific
level: Education generally (schools and universities); not HE-specific
sample: Not applicable (conceptual review)
key_findings: The standard assessment paradigm is characterised as onerous, discrete, uniform, inauthentic and antiquated (assessing skills humans now offload to computers). [Sec 2.1] | AI approaches are reviewed under five shifts: onerous to feasible (question generation, AI-assisted peer assessment, writing analytics), discrete to continuous (e-assessment logs, stealth assessment, knowledge tracing, process analytics), uniform to adaptive (computerised adaptive testing), inauthentic to authentic (AI-supported simulations such as virtual internships), and antiquated to modern (AI writing tools). [Sec 3.1-3.5] | Six challenges of AI-enabled assessment are raised: sidelining of teacher expertise, black-boxing of accountability, restricting assessment's pedagogical role, assessing limited forms of learning (including possible cultural and ableist bias), surveillance pedagogy, and distributed human-AI assessment models. [Sec 4.1-4.6] | Under evidence-centred design, AI implies assessing traits that require human contribution, allowing AI tools during tasks, and accounting for joint human-AI evidence (separating or jointly modelling contributions); prior work has focused mainly on the evidence model. [Sec 4.6] | The authors conclude AI only partially addresses traditional assessment problems and is not a panacea; it brings new challenges for assessment design and implementation. [Sec 5]
author_recommendations: Design AI-enabled assessment systems whose decisions are explainable to teachers, keeping teachers' judgement in the loop (not tested) | Establish rigorous oversight and clear lines of accountability for AI-produced assessment decisions and how they become grades (not tested) | Shift continuous monitoring toward developmental feedback rather than judgement (not tested) | Extend assessment design theory to the student and task models under human-AI teamwork, not only the evidence model (not tested)
limitations: Authors state the review is not exhaustive and highlights exemplar approaches (footnote 2). Pre-ChatGPT (2022), so it does not address current LLM capabilities. Not HE-specific. No systematic search or appraisal of included studies.
quality_note: Full text read. Clear aim; argument well grounded in cited literature; conceptual, so no data (q3 N). Scope limitation noted only in a footnote and there is no limitations section (q5 Unclear).
dim_authenticity: Argues traditional tasks are inauthentic (e.g., writing in isolation without tools) and reviews AI-supported simulations such as virtual internships as routes to authentic assessment (Sec 2.1, 3.4).
dim_capability_verification: Under human-AI teamwork the evidence model must separate or account for human versus AI contributions to assessment evidence (Sec 4.6).
dim_integrity_security: Discusses plagiarism detection (Turnitin) and exam log data for misconduct investigation, and warns that continuous AI monitoring creates surveillance that can erode trust (Sec 3.1.3, 3.2.1, 4.5).
dim_lo_alignment: Argues the student model should shift to skills requiring human contribution rather than those AI can do alone (Sec 4.6).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Suggests the task model should allow students to use AI tools during assessment, as professionals do (Sec 3.5, 4.6).
dim_scalability: AI-assisted peer assessment and automated scoring are presented as scaling to large classes and MOOCs (Sec 3.1.2-3.1.3).
dim_workload: AI can offload task generation, peer-grade aggregation and scoring from educators, but the paper warns of over-reliance on machine outputs (Sec 3.1, 4.1).
dim_feasibility: Automated question generation depends on large relevant datasets, and its metrics do not guarantee pedagogical value (Sec 3.1.1).
dim_process_visibility: Reviews AI-enabled assessment of learning processes (log, clickstream, multimodal data) rather than only final artefacts (Sec 3.2.4).
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes uniform assessments may give unequal opportunity, and AI-enabled assessment may encode Western, ableist or neurotypical norms (Sec 2.1, 4.4).

title: Computing Education in the Era of Generative AI
authors: Paul C. Denny; James E. Prather; Brett A. Becker; James Finnie-Ansley; Arto Hellas; Juho Leinonen; Andrew Luxton-Reilly; Brent N. Reeves; Eddie Antonio Santos; Sami Sarsa
ft_reason: HE introductory programming; academic integrity and the effectiveness of existing assessments under code-generation LLMs is a substantial section (Sec 2.2) alongside opportunities; refereed CACM review article, 2024.
study_design: Conceptual/review article summarising the authors' own prior empirical studies (Codex on CS1 exam questions and Rainfall variants; LLM-generated exercises and code explanations) plus wider literature
country: Multinational authors (New Zealand, USA, Ireland, Finland); summarised exam study from University of Auckland (New Zealand)
sample: Not applicable for the article overall; the summarised exam study compared Codex with 71 CS1 students on two Python exams; 350 Rainfall responses; 240 generated exercises
assessment_types: Unsupervised formats; Supervised assessment; Process evidence
key_findings: Codex scored 78.5% and 78.0% on two real CS1 Python exams, ranking 17th of 71 students (top quartile), though it struggled with tasks that banned certain language features or needed inferred ASCII formatting. [p. 3 / Sec 2.1.1 / Fig 1] | Codex produced highly varied solutions to the same prompt, and common code-plagiarism detection tools are reported to be ineffective against AI-generated code, undermining similarity-based integrity checks. [pp. 3-4 / Sec 2.1.2, 2.2, 2.2.1] | Authors anticipate institutional shifts to secure assessment conditions and possible use of keystroke/activity data, and question where acceptable machine-generated code ends and misconduct begins. [p. 4 / Sec 2.2.2] | Suggested assessment shifts include judging style/quality across multiple correct solutions, critique of AI-generated solutions, specification-focused tasks and rewarding incremental testing. [pp. 7-8 / Sec 3.3, 3.4.2, 3.4.5] | Authors conclude many existing assessment approaches may no longer be effective and argue educators must incorporate the tools and teach responsible use. [p. 9 / Sec 4]
author_recommendations: Get ahead of the tools and incorporate them into classrooms from the start, teaching responsible use (not tested) | Shift assessment toward judging quality/style across multiple solutions and critiquing AI-generated code (not tested) | Use specification-focused tasks and renewed test-driven development with rewards for incremental testing (not tested) | Teach the wider societal, legal and ethical implications of generative AI (not tested)
limitations: Not explicitly stated. The article reflects early-2023 models (Codex) and largely summarises prior studies; integrity proposals are speculative.
quality_note: Conceptual review grounded in the authors' empirical studies and cited literature; summarised studies only briefly described; no limitations section.
dim_authenticity: Argues the professional reality of AI-assisted coding should shape tasks (reading, testing, refactoring AI code).
dim_capability_verification: Codex reaching top-quartile CS1 exam scores shows typical programming assessments may no longer verify individual capability.
dim_integrity_security: Plagiarism detectors are reported ineffective on AI code and AI use is low-risk compared with contract cheating; secure conditions anticipated.
dim_lo_alignment: Questions whether code-writing outcomes remain appropriate; argues code literacy (read, test, verify) stays essential.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Raises the unresolved question of which machine-generated code suggestions are acceptable and how attribution should work.
dim_scalability: Notes LLMs could generate a near-endless supply of novel exercises, reducing the cost of fresh assessment items.
dim_workload: Generating exercises/explanations with LLMs may reduce instructor effort; filtering poor outputs is still required.
dim_process_visibility: Mentions keystroke data and incremental test-writing as possible ways to evidence student process.
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes bias in generated code and comments, and greater access for learners without formal education.

title: Incorporating Generative AI into Software Development Education
authors: Olga Petrovska; Lee Clift; Faron Moller; Rebecca Pearsall
ft_reason: Degree apprenticeship (HE) in software engineering; designs and reports formative and summative assessments built around critical evaluation of ChatGPT output; peer-reviewed ACM conference paper (published Jan 2024; DOI dated 2023); English.
study_design: Practice/experience report: three anonymous surveys plus experimental formative and summative assessments, analysed descriptively and with a coding scheme
discipline: Software engineering / computing (Applied Software Engineering Degree Apprenticeship)
level: Undergraduate (degree apprenticeship, first-year and final-year learners)
sample: Surveys: first-year learners n=12, final-year learners n=12, industry professionals n=13; experimental summative assessment: 17 first-year learners (Professional Issues module)
key_findings: The summative assessment had learners use ChatGPT to generate Java and Pep/8 Assembly code and one-sided arguments, then critique the outputs and reflect on their prompting 'journey'. The rubric marked prompt construction, rigour of analysis and ethical discussion. [Sec 3 p.2] | For a simple Java task, 94% of learners' first prompts produced compiling code. For Pep/8 Assembly only 29% obtained compilable code, and one learner did not notice the output was Python (an example of over-reliance). [Sec 4 p.3] | Most learners were critical of ChatGPT's cryptocurrency-sustainability argument (76%), rising to 81% after refinement. They judged long nuanced text generation weaker than their own work. [Sec 4 p.3] | Over 80% of all surveyed participants (learners and industry) showed some willingness for formal GenAI training. Only 2 of 13 industry respondents reported GenAI integration at their workplace. [Sec 4 p.3; Fig 1]
author_recommendations: Embed GenAI in assessments that require learners to critically evaluate AI output against their own work (implemented descriptively; learning effect not formally tested) | Develop summative assessments that give students the choice of using GenAI tools (future work; not tested) | Provide formal GenAI training within degree apprenticeship programmes (not tested)
limitations: No explicit limitations section. Small, single-programme samples (12/12/13 survey respondents; 17 assessed learners); descriptive percentages only; self-reported time estimates; no comparison group; short 4-page practice paper.
quality_note: Clear practice aim with a reasonable descriptive design for a practice report. Samples are small but described. The authors do not acknowledge limitations.
dim_authenticity: Industry partners and apprentices want GenAI skills, which motivated assessments that mirror workplace use of GenAI in software engineering.
dim_capability_verification: Designing tasks where GenAI performs poorly (Pep/8 Assembly) exposed learners' understanding and over-reliance.
dim_integrity_security: Framed as assessments that use GenAI 'without the risk of the AI tools doing the homework', by marking critique rather than the output itself; not formally evaluated.
dim_lo_alignment: Rubric criteria (prompt quality, rigour of comparison with own work, ethical analysis) target critical evaluation outcomes.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: AI use was required and scaffolded, and learners discussed professional and ethical implications of GenAI in education and work.
dim_feasibility: Implemented in a real module with 17 learners; the authors plan to extend it to more modules.
dim_process_visibility: Learners documented and reflected on their prompting 'journey', which was marked.

title: The Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS): A Framework for Ethical Integration of Generative AI in Educational Assessment
authors: Mike Perkins; Leon Furze; Jasper Roe; Jason Alexander MacVaugh
venue: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice
ft_reason: Formal framework paper for GenAI in HE assessment and integrity, peer-reviewed journal (2024, English).
study_design: Conceptual framework paper (AI Assessment Scale) grounded in a literature review
discipline: Discipline-agnostic (HE generally; notes it is applicable to K-12)
sample: Not applicable (no empirical data; the scale had only been piloted in one cohort, with no reported results)
assessment_types: Supervised assessment; Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Process evidence; AI-use declarations
key_findings: Proposes a five-level AI Assessment Scale (No AI; AI-assisted idea generation and structuring; AI-assisted editing; AI task completion with human evaluation; Full AI) so educators can set permitted GenAI use per task based on learning outcomes. [p. 7, Table 1] | Recommends that Level 1 (No AI) tasks be supervised or low-stakes formative, because unsupervised no-AI conditions raise equity concerns and AI use may be undetectable; examples include viva voce and technology-free oral discussion. [p. 8, Sec 'Level 1: No AI'] | At Level 3, students submit their original work alongside the AI-edited version, and at Level 4 any AI-created content must be cited; Level 3 is framed as a transitional stop-gap. [pp. 7, 9-10, Table 1; Sec 'Level 3' and 'Level 4'] | Argues that treating AI-generated text as inherently misconduct is unsustainable, that detection approaches are flawed, and that misuse is better handled through rubrics than as integrity breaches. [p. 4; p. 12] | Highlights unequal access to paid or advanced GenAI tools as an equity issue and suggests standardising which tools are permitted. [pp. 11-12, Sec 'Balancing Skill Development, Engagement, and Ethics']
author_recommendations: Adopt the five-level AIAS and tailor it to institutional policy (not tested). | Run Level 1 (No AI) tasks under supervision or as low-stakes formative tasks (not tested). | Develop student-facing guidelines on ethics, citation and limitations of GenAI (not tested). | Handle GenAI misuse through assessment rubrics rather than as an academic integrity breach (not tested). | Conduct empirical studies of the AIAS in diverse settings (not tested).
limitations: Authors state there is no empirical evidence of the scale's effectiveness (only a recent pilot), that it may not suit all assessments and must be adapted to learning outcomes, that it cannot stop students disguising GenAI use, and that it needs ongoing updating as the technology changes (p. 12).
quality_note: Clear aim and argument grounded in cited literature; no data, so q3 is N and q4 is Unclear (claims of effectiveness not evaluated); limitations explicitly stated.
dim_authenticity: Higher levels (L4-L5) are linked to authentic and industry-style tasks that reflect professional AI use (pp. 5, 10).
dim_capability_verification: Level 1 under supervision, including viva voce, is the route to verify unaided knowledge and skills (p. 8).
dim_integrity_security: Acknowledges the scale does not stop students disguising AI use and that detection tools are flawed (pp. 4, 12).
dim_lo_alignment: Educators choose the AIAS level according to the learning outcomes being addressed (abstract; p. 12).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: The core contribution: graded, cumulative levels that tell students where GenAI use is permitted (pp. 6-10).
dim_scalability: Presented as simple and quick to implement at institutional level and adaptable to local policy (pp. 1, 7).
dim_feasibility: Recommends supporting guidelines and multimedia material and notes the scale must be continually updated as tools evolve (pp. 8, 12).
dim_process_visibility: Level 3 requires the original work in an appendix and Level 4 requires citing AI content, which makes the process partly visible (pp. 7, 9-10).
dim_accessibility_equity: Unequal access to premium tools and to language fluency is a key concern; suggests standardising permitted tools (pp. 8, 11-13).

title: Coauthorship integrity: Reconceptualising assessment validity for the age of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Mohsen Ebrahimzadeh; Antonette Shibani; Simon Buckingham Shum
ft_reason: University context (non-proctored writing assessment); assessment validity and academic integrity are the primary focus; GenAI/LLM-based AI Viva; peer-reviewed journal article; 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Conceptual/framework paper (Coauthorship Integrity as a new source of validity evidence) plus proof-of-concept design of an LLM 'AI Viva' prototype and a preliminary expert evaluation (think-aloud, 0-10 ratings and semi-structured interviews)
discipline: Not discipline-specific (writing assessment generally); expert evaluators from linguistics, education, urban studies, futures studies and museology
level: Higher education (general); evaluation used academic staff, not students
sample: 8 expert educators at UTS (3 subject-matter experts, 5 also assessment experts; teaching experience M = 10.5 years, SD = 6.07), each evaluating the prototype on a journal paper they brought (self-authored in 7 of 8 cases); sessions about 90 min (two about 160 min)
assessment_types: Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Personalised tasks
key_findings: The authors argue that GenAI use in non-proctored writing threatens all five AERA/APA/NCME sources of validity evidence, and propose Coauthorship Integrity (whether the student can account for and defend the ideas in a possibly AI-coauthored text) as an additional, foundational source of validity evidence. [Sec 2, Sec 3, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Table 6] | The AI Viva prototype generates comprehension items (multiple-choice, matching, true/false, cloze and open-ended) from the submitter's own text across all six levels of Bloom's revised taxonomy, scores responses, gives a structured feedback report and invites follow-up dialogue. [Sec 4, Sec 5.2-5.4, Fig. 7] | Experts rated open-ended items higher for checking comprehension (means 8.38-9.00 for Remember to Analyze and Create levels) than recognition items such as multiple-choice (6.38) and cloze (6.25); perceived difficulty rose broadly from Remember to Create. [Sec 7.2-7.3, Table 3, Fig. 9] | Scoring accuracy and feedback quality were rated highly for items 1-8 (means about 8.1-9.6), and in post-viva dialogue the agent held its score of 0 for a deliberately irrelevant answer when the expert contested it; Evaluate- and Create-level answers were not scored because of time limits. [Sec 7.4-7.5, Table 3, Tables 4-5] | The authors position the AI Viva as formative only at this stage; summative use would require assessment-security measures, and preventing AI-on-AI cheating remains unresolved. [Sec 1, Sec 8.3, Sec 8.6]
author_recommendations: Adopt Coauthorship Integrity as an additional source of validity evidence for non-proctored assessment (not tested). | Use AI Vivas formatively to build students' metacognitive awareness of how they use GenAI (preliminary expert evaluation only; not tested with students). | Treat any summative use with great caution and add security measures such as identity verification and locked-down or invigilated conditions (not tested). | Ground the LLM in quality-assured sources to avoid reinforcing misconceptions in the student's text (not tested). | Develop 'AI Viva Analytics' to identify cohort misconceptions under clear privacy governance (not tested).

[Sec 4.2.1, Table 2] | Only three documents address integrating AI into assignments and pedagogical practice, and guidance rarely explains how to design for transferable skills with AI. [Sec 4.2.2, Table 2] | Assessment design considerations cluster into four themes: GenAI-integrated pedagogical dimensions, accessibility and inclusiveness, holistic design, and ethical principles (data privacy has the strongest alignment). [Sec 4.3, Table 3]
author_recommendations: Adapt curricula and build GenAI literacy, with professional development for teachers (not tested). | Ensure equitable access, data privacy and transparency in policy (not tested). | Research how higher-order thinking can be authentically assessed with GenAI (not tested).
limitations: Authors state the analysis is limited to selected IGO documents and may miss regional or local nuances; future work should include developing-country documents and empirical testing of the guidelines (Sec 5).
quality_note: Clear RQs, documented sample and thematic process, tables trace each theme to its source documents, limitations stated. Read through a WebFetch rendering of the HTML rather than a saved PDF.
dim_authenticity: Authentic assessment simulating real-world contexts is cited as a resilient design (Sec 3; Sec 4.2.1).
dim_integrity_security: Cheat-proof tests and integrity concerns appear in two documents but without operational detail (Sec 4.2.1, Table 2).
dim_lo_alignment: Synthesises the skills that policy documents want in learning outcomes (Sec 4.1, Table 1).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Advocates hybrid intelligence, where AI augments rather than replaces core cognition (Sec 5).
dim_feasibility: Calls for teacher professional development and supporting infrastructure (Sec 5, Table 4).
dim_process_visibility: Calls for assessment of both process and performance, using learner-generated evidence and reflection (Sec 3).
dim_accessibility_equity: Equity of access, technical accessibility and the digital divide are recurring themes (Sec 4.3.2, 4.3.4).

title: Embracing a new world: authentic assessment designs in an age of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)
authors: Feng Su; Michael O'Dea; Margaret Wood; Eva Seidl
venue: Perspectives: Policy and Practice in Higher Education
ft_reason: HE context; authentic assessment design in response to GenAI is the primary focus; GenAI; peer-reviewed (two anonymous reviewers acknowledged); 2026, English.
study_design: Conceptual paper informed by a rapid review (2 journals plus 2 blog platforms), with four illustrative practice scenarios
discipline: Multi-disciplinary: social sciences, translation/interpreting language education, computer science (databases), applied medical sciences
level: Undergraduate (final-year social sciences; second-year CS; second-year medical sciences); language course level not reported
sample: Rapid review: 55 articles screened, 12 included (Assessment & Evaluation in HE, IETI; 2022-2024) plus 14 blog pieces (WonkHE, THE Campus; 2023-2024). Scenario cohorts' n not reported.
assessment_types: Oral assessments; Staged submissions; Process evidence; AI-use declarations
key_findings: The authors argue that GenAI lets authenticity be reconceived as hybrid and relational, shown through transparent and purposeful student interaction with AI. [p. 2; abstract] | The review literature suggests that AI use cannot be reliably detected, that students are unclear about what use is acceptable, and that tutors may need to combine process, content analysis and direct assessment methods instead of detection tools. [pp. 5-6] | In Scenario 3 (second-year CS database module), the brief was run through ChatGPT before release. Its output was critiqued in class, students had to produce work better than it, and marks were reweighted towards process justification, evaluation and reflection. The authors report positive student response and less need for the marker to second-guess plagiarism. [Scenario 3, pp. 8-9] | In Scenario 1, students critiqued a 500-word AI response and wrote AI-free reflections, declaring the tool and prompts used. Students valued the clear guidance, but some raised concerns about unequal access to paid AI tools and inaccurate outputs. [Scenario 1, p. 7] | The authors conclude that no single solution exists ('silver buckshot'): authentic assessment should be combined with staff and student AI literacy programmes and institution-wide AI assessment frameworks such as the AIAS. [Concluding remarks, pp. 9-10]
author_recommendations: Design GenAI into authentic assessment tasks, e.g. critiquing AI outputs or outperforming an AI baseline (illustrated through scenarios, not formally evaluated) | Pre-run assessment briefs through GenAI and reweight criteria towards higher-order thinking and process (not tested) | Develop GenAI literacy for both staff and students (not tested) | Adopt an institution-wide AI assessment framework (e.g. AIAS) for clarity and transparency of AI use (not tested) | Leaders should engage with postplagiarism and generativism ideas when rethinking assessment fundamentals (not tested)
limitations: No explicit limitations section. Reviewer note: the rapid review covered only two journals and two blog platforms; scenario outcomes are anecdotal practitioner reflections with no reported n or systematic data collection.
quality_note: Clear question; conceptual argument grounded in a documented rapid review; but the scenario evidence is anecdotal with unreported samples, and no limitations are acknowledged.
dim_authenticity: Core focus: draws on Ashford-Rowe et al.'s critical elements and McArthur's social-value view, and shows authenticity through AI-integrated tasks (pp. 1-2, 6-9).
dim_capability_verification: Cites interactive orals and viva elements as a way to support integrity, and Scenario 1 requires AI-free critical reflection (pp. 4, 7).
dim_integrity_security: Argues for moving the focus from detection and misconduct towards integrating GenAI, since detection is unreliable (pp. 5-6).
dim_lo_alignment: Scenario 3 adjusted marking criteria to reward higher-order thinking and metacognition (p. 8).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Calls for clear, standardised guidance on when and how students may use GenAI, e.g. adopting the AIAS at institutional level (p. 10).
dim_workload: Cites Tight (2024): fewer but more meaningful assessments to reduce over-assessment (p. 5).
dim_feasibility: Scenario 3 reports that adapting an existing authentic assessment needed only a relatively simple change to the marking criteria (p. 8).
dim_process_visibility: Scenarios require prompt/tool declarations and reward descriptions of process and justification of decisions (pp. 7-8).
dim_accessibility_equity: Raises unequal access to premium AI tools and the potential of GenAI to support students with disabilities such as dyslexia (pp. 4, 6-7).

title: Changing EAP assessment practices in the age of generative artificial intelligence: The case of Scottish higher education institutions
authors: Lewis Urquhart; Xuan Minh Ngo
venue: Journal of English for Academic Purposes
ft_reason: HE (Scottish universities' EAP provision); assessment change in response to GenAI is the primary focus; peer reviewed; 2025/2026.
study_design: Qualitative case study; semi-structured interviews; thematic analysis
discipline: English for Academic Purposes (pre-sessional and in-sessional/integrated)
sample: 6 EAP academics in leadership roles at 5 Scottish universities, interviewed mid-2024; purposive sampling; institutional websites used to triangulate
assessment_types: Supervised assessment; Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Staged submissions; Process evidence; Personalised tasks; AI-use declarations
key_findings: The five departments made few changes to core task types. Adaptations were mostly to task requirements (GenAI declarations, context-specific prompts such as local case studies, next-day follow-up Q&A after presentations) and to grading. [p. 5-6, Sec 4.1; Table 4] | Grading changes included more weight on contextual relevance than linguistic accuracy, and a switch from anonymised to named marking by course tutors. The tutor-marker change was well received and reportedly coincided with fewer misconduct cases. [p. 6, Sec 4.1-4.2] | Three participants judged GenAI use declarations ineffective. One saw them mainly as an institutional safeguard for imposing penalties, not a deterrent. [p. 6, Sec 4.2] | Participants mostly favoured authentic and innovative tasks (portfolios with a viva element, reflections, multimodal work, evaluating GenAI output) over a return to exams, but raised workload concerns about marking multiple drafts and doubts that portfolios resist GenAI. [p. 6-7, Sec 4.3; p. 8, Sec 5.2] | The authors argue that unchanged essays, reports and presentations put the validity of inferences about independent language ability at risk. They attribute slow change to time, approval bureaucracy and staffing pressures. [p. 7, Sec 5.1]
author_recommendations: Institutions should support small-scale pilots of innovative or GenAI-integrated assessment (not tested). | Allocate redesign time, streamline assessment amendment approvals, and provide professional development on designing and validating GenAI-resilient assessments (not tested). | Run ongoing professional dialogue and bottom-up development drawing on EAP practitioners' expertise (not tested). | Adopt iterative, locally divergent redesign rather than one-size-fits-all solutions (not tested).
limitations: Small sample (6 participants, 5 institutions, two from one university) at one point in mid-2024, so findings may not generalise. Relies on interview recall, with partial triangulation from websites; some contextual data (student numbers) could not be verified.
quality_note: Clear RQs; appropriate qualitative case design with member checking, an audit trail and researcher triangulation; sample and context described (Tables 1-2); themes supported by quotes; limitations stated (p. 9). The sample is very small.
dim_authenticity: Practitioners rejected pen-and-paper exams as inauthentic and favoured authentic, innovative and multimodal tasks.
dim_capability_verification: Follow-up Q&A after presentations and spontaneous speaking tasks were used to verify mastery of content.
dim_integrity_security: Declarations were seen as ineffective; named marking by tutors who know the students was seen as more effective.
dim_lo_alignment: Concern that GenAI integration may require skills beyond EAP outcomes, and that unchanged tasks threaten valid inferences about language ability.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Divided views on integrating GenAI; evaluating GenAI output was being trialled in some programmes.
dim_workload: Marking multiple drafts and redesigning assessments were constrained by time, hiring freezes and course-approval processes.
dim_feasibility: Institutional bureaucracy and the need for academic board approval slowed changes to task types.
dim_process_visibility: Process-oriented elements (drafts, portfolios, follow-up Q&A) were emerging only as incremental adjustments.

title: Online assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
authors: Alexander Stanoyevitch
ft_reason: HE online exam integrity with ChatGPT and exam-help platforms, plus strategies including for CS/coding questions; peer-reviewed case study 2024.
study_design: Single-instructor retrospective observational case study of exam grade distributions, plus in-exam item-modification experiments and experience-based recommendations
discipline: Mathematics/statistics; upper-level machine learning course with programming (R)
sample: Introductory statistics large lecture of 120-150 students per semester (2020-2021 online semesters); upper-level ML course of 20-30 students; exact n per exam not reported
assessment_types: Unsupervised formats; Supervised assessment; Oral assessments
key_findings: Unproctored online multiple-choice exams produced markedly higher grades than the same exams in person; reusing an old exam online gave a distribution where A was the most common grade. [pp. 6-7 / Sec 4.1 / Figs 2-4] | When a parameter was changed so the old correct option became wrong, on average 72% of students chose the previously correct answer, indicating reliance on exam-help platforms. [p. 7 / Sec 4.1] | The ChatGPT-specific evidence is one example: ChatGPT solved a standard dice question but failed a modified version; most quantitative data predate ChatGPT. [pp. 8-9 / Sec 4.2] | Recommendations for online exams: no question reuse, tight time limits, screening questions in ChatGPT, and using graphics/unusual symbols; the author notes this adds preparation effort. [p. 9 / Sec 4.3] | For coding questions, require executable code using only taught constructs, with possible follow-up oral explanation, or cap marks for non-compliant code. [p. 10 / Sec 5]
author_recommendations: Never reuse exam questions; write new or parameter-modified items (partly tested via in-course experiments) | Impose strict exam time limits to deter live tutoring (not formally tested) | Screen exam questions with ChatGPT and replace those it answers correctly (not tested) | Require executable code limited to taught constructs, with oral explanation if in doubt (not formally evaluated)
limitations: Author acknowledges an observational design without randomisation and alternative explanations (e.g., better home study). Further: single instructor, no inferential statistics, ChatGPT evidence is anecdotal, and the abstract's pre/post-ChatGPT framing is not matched by the data (mainly pandemic-era).
quality_note: Observational grade comparisons without statistical testing; ChatGPT claims rest on a single example.
dim_authenticity: Concludes assessment should shift from rote recall toward analysis, application and synthesis.
dim_capability_verification: Proposes calling students in to explain code that goes beyond the constructs taught.
dim_integrity_security: Shows unproctored online exams were heavily compromised; lockdown browsers can be bypassed and malfunction for about 2-3% of students.
dim_lo_alignment: Course-specific vocabulary and taught constructs used to anchor questions to course teaching.
dim_scalability: Strategies were applied in a large lecture of 120-150 students using automated MC grading.
dim_workload: Integrity measures need substantial extra question-writing effort, traded against saved grading time.
dim_feasibility: Lockdown browser issues required special accommodations and instructor availability during exams.
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes harder/shorter exams risk penalising honest students, and lockdown failures affect students through no fault of their own.

title: Is AI changing learning and assessment as we know it? Evidence from a ChatGPT experiment and a conceptual framework
authors: Oluwaseun Kolade; Adebowale Owoseni; Abiodun Egbetokun
ft_reason: HE essay assessment validity and integrity under ChatGPT (plagiarism checks, human grading) plus a framework for AI-assisted assessment; peer-reviewed; 2024; English.
study_design: Quasi-experiment (ChatGPT-generated essays tested with Turnitin, Grammarly and two human markers) followed by a conceptual framework
sample: Purposive sample of Masters social-science students (reported as 20 students and 33 essay outputs in Stage 2, but 18 participants and 23 essays in Stages 1 and 4; Table 1 lists S1-S20 and E1-E33); two PhD-holding lecturers as assessors
key_findings: Turnitin similarity was low for essays from distinct accounts (mostly under 25%). Repeat essays from the same account with the same prompt rose to 86-99%, so Turnitin was not effective for AI essays generated across multiple accounts. [Sec 4.1 p.6; Table 1 pp.7-9] | Human markers rated many AI essays satisfactory to good (scores roughly 40-77.6%), but noted missing theory, case examples and citations, and judged some essays similar in substance despite low Turnitin similarity. [Sec 4.1 p.6; Table 1 pp.7-9] | All citations and references ChatGPT supplied for the essay and report could not be found (placeholder or fabricated references). [Sec 5 p.12; footnote 2 p.12; Table 2 p.11] | The authors propose an AI-assisted assessment framework based on Miller's pyramid, extending assessment from knowledge (know what) to competence (know how) and performance (show how). It has six propositions (chatbot feedback, automated essay scoring, adaptive feedback/testing, serious games). [Sec 5.1 pp.12-14; Fig 4]
author_recommendations: Use AI chatbots for formative feedback and automated essay scoring for summative knowledge assessment (not tested) | Use AI-assisted adaptive feedback and adaptive testing for competence-level assessment (not tested) | Use computer serious games for formative and summative performance assessment (not tested) | Higher education providers should embrace rather than resist AI and rethink essay-centred assessment (not tested)
limitations: Authors note: possible topic and geographic effects of the single prompt; straightforward prompts with a single run (no iteration); no comparison with student-written essays; single discipline (p.15). Further issues: inconsistent counts of participants and essays; assessors were drawn from the authors' network; the framework is not derived from or tested against the experimental data.
quality_note: Clear RQs and appropriate exploratory quasi-experiment, but the sample and essay counts are internally inconsistent (18 vs 20 participants; 23 vs 33 essays). The framework is conceptual and untested.
dim_authenticity: Argues assessment should move beyond essays to competence and performance in simulated real-life contexts (e.g., serious games).
dim_capability_verification: Shows that essays can be produced by ChatGPT at passable-to-good quality, weakening essays as evidence of individual capability.
dim_integrity_security: Shows Turnitin missed AI-generated essays from distinct accounts and AI detectors were imprecise; human markers spotted some content similarity.
dim_lo_alignment: Framework aligns assessment levels with Miller's know what / know how / show how outcomes.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Advocates accepting and supporting student AI use while restructuring assessment toward higher levels.
dim_scalability: Proposes automated essay scoring and adaptive testing to reduce staff time at scale (untested).
dim_workload: Notes that manual expert scrutiny for AI-generated work is time-consuming and adds workload.
dim_feasibility: Acknowledges operationalising the framework needs systemic change and may face stakeholder resistance.
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes work-based placements are resource-intensive and unequally available, motivating AI simulations.

title: AI in action: Changes to student perceptions when using generative artificial intelligence for the creation of a multimedia project-based assessment
authors: Kellie A. Charles; Arsalan Yousuf; Han Chow Chua; Slade T. Matthews; Joanna Harnett; Tina Hinton
ft_reason: Final-year undergraduate capstone unit; pilots an AI-permitted authentic group multimedia assessment and examines AI use and assessment integrity (substantial focus); GenAI; peer-reviewed journal; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study (constructivist paradigm) of one unit; abductive thematic analysis of routinely collected LMS data (pre-semester Padlet posts and group project logbooks) using Messeri and Crockett's four AI personas; frequencies of personas reported
discipline: Pharmacology (capstone interdisciplinary research unit PCOL3888, Bachelor of Science)
sample: 40 enrolled students contributed Padlet posts (4355 words; 71 persona descriptions); 2 withdrew, leaving 38 students in 5 project groups of 7-8; 14 AI use cases from the logbooks of 4 groups (one group reported no AI use); semester 2, 2023
key_findings: AI use was permitted in all assessments except reflections, provided students acknowledged the tools and described their prompts and how outputs were integrated; the group logbook recorded roles, meetings, decisions and AI use. [Sec 2.1, Sec 2.3.2, Fig. 1] | Before the projects, students mostly saw AI in a tutor-like Arbiter role (49%), then Oracle (41%) and Quant (10%); 70% described two or more roles and none described AI as a Surrogate. [Sec 3.2, Fig. 2A] | Actual use was low to moderate and confined mainly to idea generation (Oracle, 12 of 14 cases, 86%) and data analysis (Quant, 2 cases, 14%); no group used AI as an Arbiter or to write text for the final submission. [Sec 3.3, Table 2, Fig. 2B] | All projects reached distinction or above (over 85%) and were submitted with AI acknowledgements, but only one group fully documented prompts and outputs with evidence of evaluative judgement; two groups did so only partially. [Sec 3.3, Table 2] | The authors attribute the gap between perceived and actual use to student uncertainty, including conflicting messages from other units equating AI use with plagiarism, and call for assessing the learning process and students' evaluative judgement of AI outputs. [Sec 4, Sec 5]
author_recommendations: Pilot assessments that explicitly acknowledge and incorporate AI use (not tested beyond this single pilot). | Assess the learning process and students' evaluative judgement of AI outputs, not just the product (not tested). | Provide clear guidance to educators and students on assessing AI-supported learning (not tested). | Expand professional development in AI literacy for educators and share exemplars of AI integration (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge: a small cohort of final-year science students in one specialised unit; few AI use cases; findings may reflect the early stage of AI tools in late 2023 (Sec 4.1). Also noted: the two withdrawn students' anonymous Padlet posts could not be removed; researchers taught the unit (reflexivity statement, Sec 2.6); no explicit AI guidance was given to students.
quality_note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear aims; case study design with a theory-based coding framework, multiple coders and a reflexivity statement; sample and data sources well described; findings are supported by frequencies and use-case table; limitations section present. Small single-unit, non-computing sample limits transfer.
dim_authenticity: The group multimedia education-campaign project was designed on authentic and sustainable assessment principles to mirror research and professional roles (Sec 1, Sec 2.1, Sec 4).
dim_integrity_security: Authors argue that clear guidance on assessing AI-supported process is needed to protect assessment integrity, and that bans, detectors or full return to invigilated tasks are not feasible for large science units (Abstract, Sec 4).
dim_lo_alignment: Unit learning outcomes are mapped to university graduate qualities, including digital literacy (Appendix 1, Table 2).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: AI was openly encouraged with acknowledgement, yet students used it sparingly and mainly for brainstorming, suggesting uncertainty about appropriate use (Sec 3.3, Sec 4).
dim_feasibility: Supervisors had limited AI know-how, so no guidance on specific tools or teaching on how to use them was given (Sec 2.1).
dim_process_visibility: Logbooks with AI-use descriptions made the process visible, but documentation quality varied, with only one group fully detailing inputs, outputs and judgements (Sec 2.3.2, Sec 3.3).
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes that students more confident in academic writing, including native speakers, may be less likely to use AI (Sec 4).

title: Generative AI in computing education: A systematic review and a framework for responsible integration
authors: Arun Kumar; Thakerng Wongsirichot; Aziz Nanthaamornphong
ft_reason: Systematic review of GenAI in computing/programming education, primarily HE; RQ3 on assessment redesign and integrity is a substantial strand (AI-resistant assessment is the densest theme); peer-reviewed journal (CAEAI); 2026; English.
study_design: Systematic literature review (Kitchenham & Charters; Wohlin snowballing from 7 seeds; PRISMA 2020 reporting) with 10-item quality appraisal, thematic synthesis (Cruzes & Dyba) and a derived framework (VIE)
country: Not applicable (review); authors based in India and Thailand; corpus mainly North America, Northern Europe and Australasia
level: Primarily higher education (CS1 30 studies, mixed 34, intermediate 5, advanced 3); limited secondary/vocational coverage
sample: 72 primary studies (2022-2026) from 33 venues, out of 99 candidates; mean QA 8.32/10; 61 full-weight studies
assessment_types: Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Practical demonstrations; Staged submissions; Process evidence; AI-use declarations
key_findings: Thirteen studies show most standard programming assessments can be completed by current GenAI. Visual-spatial tasks and under-specified problems are partial exceptions, and one study found authentic context-specific tasks had 41% AI completion versus 82% for standard exam tasks. [Sec 4.2.4, Sec 4.4.1, Table 5] | AI-resistant assessment design is the most densely evidenced theme (26 studies). Strategies include process-visible work (staged portfolios, code journals), oral defence/viva and live coding (endorsed by 12 studies), authentic contextualised tasks, Prompt Problems and perturbation. [Sec 4.4.5, Fig. 7] | Self-reported undisclosed AI use on assessments is commonly 45-65% (13 studies). Policy ambiguity predicts it, and peer norms were the strongest predictor of misconduct intention in one SEM study. [Sec 4.4.2, Sec 4.4.4] | AI detection is thinly evidenced (3 studies). The best result reported was 89% accuracy with an 8% false-positive rate. The authors argue false positives fall unevenly on students such as non-native speakers and that accuracy decays across model generations. [Sec 4.4.3] | The VIE framework (Verification, Implementation, Equity) requires graded, observable critical engagement with AI output, institutional capacity (policy, faculty development, assessment redesign) and equity-aware design. Each is treated as interdependent. [Sec 5.1, Fig. 8]
author_recommendations: Redesign at least one high-stakes assessment per course to include an oral component or process-visible element (not tested by the review) | Introduce GenAI gradually after foundational competence, with course-level differentiated access policies (not tested by the review) | Teach AI literacy explicitly, including prompt engineering and AI error analysis (not tested by the review) | Prefer assessment redesign and norm-shifting (honour codes, pledges, modelled disclosure) over detection-centric enforcement (not tested) | Invest in tiered, role-aware faculty development and equity-of-access policies; address seven research gaps such as longitudinal and cross-national studies (not tested)
limitations: Snowballing from 7 seeds may miss papers outside citation chains; English-only; screening and QA by a single rater (second coder for thematic coding only on 18 studies, kappa 0.62); QA for some papers without full text was based on venue and extraction data; Table 4 counts flagged as needing re-tally after the supplementary search; constructs are heterogeneously operationalised; corpus skewed to English-speaking, well-resourced contexts.
quality_note: Explicit RQs, protocol, PRISMA flow, QA instrument, IRR and replication package; corpus well described (Tables 2-4). Threats to validity discussed in depth. Minor concerns: single-rater screening/QA and an internally inconsistent Table 4 note.
dim_authenticity: Authentic, context-specific tasks needing local knowledge are among the most AI-resistant strategies; one primary study showed roughly half the AI completion rate of standard tasks (Sec 4.4.1, Sec 4.4.5).
dim_capability_verification: Finds submitted code no longer reliably shows skill; oral defence and live coding are the most AI-resistant in practice because they require real-time independent reasoning (Sec 1, Sec 4.4.5).
dim_integrity_security: Synthesises assessment vulnerability, misconduct prevalence (45-65%), weak detection and policy landscape; argues redesign and norm-shifting outperform detection-centric enforcement (Sec 4.4).
dim_lo_alignment: Argues GenAI fuses tool use, learning and assessment in computing, so artefact-based assessment cannot separate learning from delegation (Sec 1).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Recommends graduated, competence-gated AI access and explicit AI literacy; notes a contested minority view favouring fully AI-permitted assessment (Sec 4.4.5, Sec 4.5.1, Sec 4.5.2).
dim_workload: Fig. 7 positions strategies by implementation effort; code-explanation components are a lower-effort entry point than oral defence; AI-assisted grading reported to reduce instructor workload (Sec 4.4.5, Fig. 7).
dim_feasibility: Faculty workshops produced oral-defence and portfolio templates rated implementable within one semester; faculty development is a documented gap (Sec 4.5.4, Sec 5.4).
dim_process_visibility: Process-visible assessments (staged portfolios, code journals, think-aloud) and IDE/prompt-log analytics are proposed to make verification observable, subject to privacy and consent (Sec 4.4.5, Sec 5.5).
dim_accessibility_equity: Equity is a co-equal VIE requirement covering skill-gap and resource-gap mechanisms; detector false positives may disproportionately affect non-native speakers (Sec 4.4.3, Sec 5.1).

title: Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors
authors: Dan Kohen-Vacs; Maya Usher; Marc Jansen
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
ft_reason: HE programming courses; Study 2 evaluates exam tasks built from LLM-generated flawed code (assessment design/validity); GenAI; peer reviewed; 2025.
study_design: Two quantitative studies: cross-sectional survey (Study 1); comparison of exam task scores with paired t-tests (Study 2)
discipline: Computer science / programming (Operations Research and Cryptography courses in Study 2)
sample: Study 1: 64 undergraduates in Israel (online questionnaire, March 2024; 83% female). Study 2: 147 undergraduates in Germany, exam scores from 6 exams over 3 terms (Winter 2022/23 to Winter 2023/24; 81% male)
key_findings: In Summer 2023 and Winter 2023/24, students scored significantly lower on exam tasks that required correcting LLM-generated flawed Java code than on instructor-designed tasks, in both courses. [p. 3177; Table 6 p. 3178] | In Winter 2022/23 there was no significant difference, but overall performance was low that term (pass rates 20% and 29.41%), which the authors say may have masked differences. [p. 3178] | Students rated GenAI as useful (M=3.63), creativity-enhancing (M=3.66) and intended to keep using it (M=3.92), all significantly above neutral. Overall concerns (M=2.98) did not differ from neutral. [pp. 3175-3177; Tables 2-5] | Over-reliance was the highest-rated concern (M=3.66). Concerns about teamwork and social interaction were rated lower. [p. 3176-3177; Table 5] | The authors note the LLM debugging task was used in a high-stakes summative exam with no prior training, which may partly explain the performance gap. [pp. 3179-3180]
author_recommendations: Pair instructor-designed tasks with LLM-generated debugging challenges to build error-correction skills gradually (not tested). | Embed explicit instruction on GenAI limitations, biases and ethics, and have students critique and refine AI outputs (not tested). | Use scaffolded, guided integration of GenAI before high-stakes use (not tested). | Institutions should provide professional development and clear policies on integrity, privacy and over-reliance (not tested).
limitations: Two populations from different countries limit generalisability. Study 2 compares tasks with different cognitive demands (debugging vs construction). The design is short-term, and pedagogical integration strategies were not examined (pp. 3180-3181).
quality_note: Clear RQs, appropriate quantitative methods, samples described, and limitations stated. q4 is Unclear: score scales and normalisation between task types are not fully clear (e.g. traditional SDs exceed means), and the task comparison is confounded by task type.
dim_authenticity: Frames correcting AI-generated code as a skill students need for AI-augmented development work.
dim_capability_verification: Invigilated exam tasks requiring correction of LLM-generated code exposed gaps in debugging and foundational skill.
dim_lo_alignment: Authors note the LLM debugging task and the construction tasks measure different cognitive demands, which limits comparability.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Students reported positive views and strong intention to use GenAI, with over-reliance as their main worry; authors call for explicit instruction on GenAI limits.

title: Impact of ChatGPT on learning outcomes and performance of students in computer programming courses: a mixed-method approach
authors: Omobola O. Gambo; Olabamiji John Onifade; Wasiu. Olanrewaju-Smart; Odianose John Abuya; Rukayat Enitan Salawu; Rhodes Massenon; Ishaya Gambo
ft_reason: Primary focus is ChatGPT's effect on learning outcomes, perceptions and scores; assessment design/validity and integrity are only touched on through a few instructor items (reliance, code similarity) and future-work remarks, not a substantial focus.
