key_findings: Students reported positive perceptions (enjoyment mean 3.93, motivation 3.75, confidence 3.72 on 5-point scales). [pp. 17-18 / Sec 4.1.1 / Fig 4] | ChatGPT-related perceptions did not predict programming scores (R2 = 0.006, no significant predictors). [pp. 23-24 / Sec 4.2.3; also p. 16 / Sec 3.7.4] | Instructors strongly agreed that students rely on ChatGPT solutions without understanding them (mean 4.29) and often saw significant similarities in submitted code (mean 3.94). [pp. 25-26 / Sec 4.3.1 / Figs 10-11] | Authors call for new assessment frameworks that can separate genuine understanding from AI-assisted outputs. [p. 31 / Sec 6]
author_recommendations: Develop assessment frameworks that distinguish genuine understanding from AI-assisted output (not tested) | Use assignments that require students to critically evaluate, refine or justify AI-generated content (not tested) | Conduct experimental/longitudinal multi-institution studies (not tested)
limitations: Authors note cross-sectional design, self-report bias, single institution and course, few instructors, low R2, non-normal residuals and ceiling effects. Also, it is unclear how anonymous survey responses were linked to scores, and Sec 3.7.5 overstates effects given the non-significant regression.
quality_note: Linkage of scores to the anonymous survey is unclear; some interpretations (Sec 3.7.5) are not supported by the non-significant results.
dim_capability_verification: The gap between perceived usefulness and scores, plus instructor reports of reliance without understanding, suggests assignments may not verify capability.
dim_integrity_security: Instructors report frequent code similarity across submissions and integrity concerns; not directly measured.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Calls for guidelines on responsible use and structured integration of ChatGPT.
dim_scalability: Large cohort of 1889 students across four faculties.

title: ChatGPT in the Classroom: Evaluating its Role in Fostering Critical Evaluation Skills
authors: Angela Oates; Donna M. Johnson
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 35: 1793-1824
ft_reason: Master's-level HE assessment redesign where students generate an essay with ChatGPT and then critically evaluate it; examines assessment quality, marks and integrity perceptions; peer-reviewed; 2025; English.
study_design: Mixed-methods pilot: marks comparison (paired t-test vs. course averages) plus focus group and questionnaire with thematic analysis
discipline: Biomedical science (Medical Microbiology, Medical Biochemistry, Biomedical Science)
sample: 10 volunteer Master's students (4 native, 6 non-native English speakers); one ~1 h focus group; questionnaire
key_findings: ChatGPT-generated essay marks (mean 66) did not differ significantly from participants' course averages. Critical evaluation marks (mean 73) were significantly higher than course averages (paired t-test p=0.04, mean difference 9%). [Results p.1805; Table 3] | AI essays had high-quality English and PEEL-style structure but lacked depth, were repetitive, and contained references that did not exist. Verifying references was the main concern in all critical evaluations. [Results pp.1805-1806] | Students preferred writing their own essays. They raised integrity concerns (AI text evading detection) and fairness concerns about paid tools, and wanted explicit guidelines and training on AI use in assessment. [Focus group pp.1807-1809; questionnaire pp.1809-1812] | Authors suggest educators use GenAI to generate materials for students to critically evaluate, and note that marks may partly reflect students' prompting skill, implying a need for new assessment criteria. [Discussion pp.1814, 1816]
author_recommendations: Have educators use GenAI to generate essays, case studies or data sets for students to critically evaluate (not tested) | Add a stage where students present arguments and counter-arguments to AI for feedback (not tested) | Develop assessment criteria that account for students' interaction with AI, e.g., prompt quality (not tested) | Provide clear institutional guidelines and training on acceptable AI use in assessment (not tested) | Investigate how levels of instructional support affect students' critical use of AI (future work)
limitations: Authors note a small sample (n=10), relatively homogeneous, motivated and tech-savvy volunteers (self-selection bias), and a possible ceiling effect from high-performing students (pp.1820-1821). Further issues: no control group; comparison is with course averages and similar assessment types; the authors both designed the task and marked it.
quality_note: Clear aim and well-described context. With n=10 and a comparison against course averages rather than a control, the design is weak for causal claims. Limitations are discussed thoroughly.
dim_authenticity: Critical evaluation of AI-generated content is framed as a skill valued in professional STEM and healthcare work.
dim_capability_verification: Marking the student's critique of the AI essay, rather than the essay itself, made students' own evaluative ability the thing being assessed.
dim_integrity_security: Participants saw AI-generated text as able to evade traditional integrity checks; the design embeds AI use rather than policing it.
dim_lo_alignment: Rubrics weighted critical analysis at 50% of the evaluation mark, matching the programme's emphasis on critical evaluation.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Orientation session covered ChatGPT limitations and integrity; students wanted explicit guidelines on acceptable AI use in assessments.
dim_workload: Estimated student workload 10-15 h over four weeks; cross-checking references offset AI time savings.
dim_feasibility: Piloted outside normal assessment with volunteers; the authors suggest AI-generated assessment content could save educator time.
dim_process_visibility: Students had to submit their prompts with their essay and evaluation; prompt types were analysed.
dim_accessibility_equity: Participants raised unequal access to paid AI tools as a fairness concern.

title: Making sense of generative AI for assessments: Contrasting student claims and assessor evaluations
authors: Isabel Fischer; Simon Sweeney; Matthew Lucas; Neha Gupta
venue: The International Journal of Management Education
ft_reason: HE postgraduate assessment with GenAI use built in and AI-use reflection; compares student claims with assessor evaluation; peer-reviewed (2024, English).
study_design: Exploratory single case study (Yin); inductive qualitative content analysis with descriptive quantification of submissions
sample: 118 reflective essays from 118 postgraduate students, one module, May 2023
assessment_types: Unsupervised formats; Process evidence; AI-use declarations
key_findings: The three-part authentic assessment (blog post, board briefing, 500-word AI-use reflection) required students to append the prompts and GenAI conversations they used. [p. 3, Sec 2.1.1; Fig. 2] | Students' claims put 26.3% at sensemaking stage 1, 56.8% at stage 2 and 16.9% at stage 3; assessors placed 20.3%, 69.5% and 10.2% respectively, so only about one in ten showed critical evaluation of AI. [pp. 6-7, Sec 3.1-3.2; Tables 4-5] | 16 of 118 students claimed to have used a bespoke tool that no student had requested access to, some describing feedback it could not have given, which suggests that AI-use reflections can be fabricated. [p. 8, Sec 3.3] | Higher assessor-rated sensemaking stages went with modestly higher marks (+2.6% at stage 2 and +3.5% at stage 3 relative to stage 1). [p. 7, Table 5] | Students most often named accuracy of results (32.2%) and lack of critical thinking (23.7%) as GenAI drawbacks; plagiarism (6.8%) and privacy (3.4%) were rarely raised. [p. 7, Table 3]
author_recommendations: Avoid or broaden lists of example tools in assignment briefs to reduce performative claims (not tested). | Use more directive brief language to encourage interpretive reflection (not tested). | Consider providing GenAI-generated model answers that students must exceed (not tested). | Develop programme-level synoptic assessments and test language proficiency independently (not tested). | Develop institutional AI strategies, AI literacy and staff professional development (not tested).
limitations: Authors note students may have written what they thought assessors wanted to hear, findings are context-specific (pre-experience Master's students, one UK business school, end-of-year timing with possible assessment fatigue) (p. 12, Sec 6). The single cross-sectional cohort limits replicability (p. 5, Sec 2.4).
quality_note: Clear aim, appropriate case design, sample and data collection described, findings tabulated, limitations stated. Coding reliability statistics are not reported.
dim_authenticity: Assessment designed to mirror real-world audiences (publishable blog, board briefing) (p. 3, Sec 2.1.1).
dim_capability_verification: Student self-reports of AI use did not match assessors' evaluation of demonstrated use (p. 8, Sec 3.3; Fig. 5).
dim_integrity_security: Fabricated claims of tool use show the limits of self-declaration as an integrity mechanism (p. 8).
dim_lo_alignment: Assessment criteria (comprehension, analysis, critical evaluation, writing) mapped to Bloom's and Driscoll's models (pp. 3-4, Fig. 3).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: School policy lets lecturers forbid, authorise or encourage GenAI; this module encouraged it (p. 2, p. 3).
dim_process_visibility: Prompts and conversations appended to submissions gave assessors evidence of the process (p. 3).
dim_accessibility_equity: Notes concern about free versus paid GenAI access and disadvantage for students with weaker language skills (p. 9).

title: Using Generative AI to Promote Psychological, Feedback, and Artificial Intelligence Literacies in Undergraduate Psychology
authors: Jenny L. Richmond; Kate Nicholls
ft_reason: Full text confirms undergraduate psychology (HE) assessment redesign integrating ChatGPT, evaluated with cohort data; peer-reviewed journal (Teaching of Psychology; online 2024, issue 2025); English. Non-computing but meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Teaching-practice evaluation: description of a three-phase assessment redesign; analysis of students' rubric grades of ChatGPT output (chi-square) and comparison of grades with the previous peer-review cohort (t-tests); non-randomised historical comparison
sample: n = 363 undergraduates (Term 1 2023; opt-out consent, none opted out); comparison cohort Term 1 2022 gradebook data, N = 397 (waiver of consent)
key_findings: Phase 1 of the three-phase Media Assignment was redesigned: students had ChatGPT draft a media release, graded it against the script-revision rubric and listed three strengths, weaknesses and revision priorities (10%); Phase 2 revised it with tracked changes (20%); the Phase 3 final video (30%) was unchanged. [Introduction; Table 1] | Students rated ChatGPT's draft highly for Style (92% above Pass) but poorly for Aims/Methods/Results (94% Credit or lower); the association between criterion and grade was large (chi-square(4) = 317.48, p < .001, adjusted Cramer's V = 0.66). [Results; Figures 1-2] | Students performed well on the AI critique task (mean 72.7; 44% Distinction or High Distinction), though a few gave ChatGPT high grades for Aims/Methods/Results, suggesting some need more scaffolding to check accuracy. [Results; Figure 3; Discussion] | Script revision grades were higher than in the 2022 peer-review cohort (69.4 vs 66.7; t(733.05) = 4.93, p < .001, d = 0.36), but final video grades did not differ (71.2 vs 70.3; p = .129). [Results; Table 2] | The authors are cautious: gains may reflect early rubric engagement or simply revising stylistically strong AI text. They note revising draws on different competencies from writing, and argue assessment should evidence the learning process rather than the artefact. [Discussion]
author_recommendations: Have students critique a GenAI draft against the marking rubric early in a staged assessment (evaluated in this course) | Provide more scaffolding for verifying the accuracy of GenAI output (not tested) | Consider having students reflect on the AI draft and then write their own draft rather than revise the AI text (planned for next implementation; not tested) | Shift assessment toward the learning process, with LMS tools for version control and process documentation (not tested)
limitations: Non-randomised comparison with the previous cohort; the authors cannot rule out that gains came from revising stylistically good AI text rather than rubric engagement. Only two of six rubric criteria are reported. No demographic data (sex and age estimated from school norms). Single course and institution.
quality_note: Full text read. Clear aims and hypotheses; appropriate descriptive and inferential analysis for a teaching evaluation; sample and data collection described with ethics; claims cautious; the key limitation (confounded cohort comparison) is acknowledged in the Discussion.
dim_authenticity: Science-communication task for a lay audience, with multi-source feedback, emulating professional writing (Introduction).
dim_integrity_security: The original task was judged at risk because ChatGPT is good at summarising and style; the redesign makes AI use mandatory and visible rather than prohibited (Introduction).
dim_lo_alignment: Students applied the actual marking rubric to AI output early, aligning critique with the criteria for later phases (Table 1; Discussion).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: GenAI use was required for the first draft and scaffolded through critique and tracked-change revision (Introduction; Table 1).
dim_scalability: Implemented in a large course (n = 363) with tutorial instructors marking (Method).
dim_feasibility: Replaced the peer-review step with an AI-critique step within an existing three-phase assessment; materials shared on OSF (Table 1).
dim_process_visibility: Tracked changes on the AI draft and an optional rejoinder document how students revised; authors call for LMS version control to document process (Table 1; Discussion).
dim_accessibility_equity: ChatGPT drafts of consistent quality made the review step more equitable than reviewing peers' variable drafts (Discussion).

title: Perceived impact of generative AI on assessments: Comparing educator and student perspectives in Australia, Cyprus, and the United States
authors: René F. Kizilcec; Elaine Huber; Elena C. Papanastasiou; Andrew Cram; Christos Andreas Makridis; Adele Smolansky; Sandris Zeivots; Corina Raduescu
ft_reason: HE (three universities); perceived impact of GenAI on assessment and preferences for assessment adaptation are the primary focus; peer reviewed; 2024.
study_design: Cross-sectional international survey with scenario-based items; mixed methods (descriptive/regression analysis plus thematic coding of open responses)
discipline: Multiple (Engineering, Business, Education, Arts and Science, Life/Health, Law)
sample: 680 students (353 Australia, 276 Cyprus, 51 US) and 87 educators (29, 48, 10) at the University of Sydney, University of Nicosia and Cornell; convenience samples surveyed in spring 2023 via Qualtrics/SurveyMonkey
key_findings: Educators and students rated coding assignments and essays as most affected by GenAI (students also rated short-answer and MCQ). Real-time presentations were expected to be least affected. [p. 5-6, Sec 4.2; Fig 1] | 67% of educators preferred the GenAI-adapted prompt (evaluate or edit ChatGPT output) over the original, against 16% for the original. Students were more divided: 41% adapted, 33% original. [p. 6, Sec 4.4; Fig 2] | Respondents judged that GenAI availability lowered the original prompts' quality on most of the six dimensions (academic integrity, authenticity, feedback, etc.) and that the adapted prompts recovered this loss. [p. 7, Sec 4.5; Fig 3] | Educators rated academic integrity slightly more important than the other quality dimensions. Students who preferred the original prompts cited integrity, creativity and original-contribution concerns. [p. 7-8, Sec 4.5; Fig 4] | Most respondents expected students to use GenAI to generate whole essays or code; students more often expected help-seeking uses such as ideas, revision and error-checking. [p. 5-6, Sec 4.3; Table 5]
author_recommendations: Institutions should run pilots of GenAI-integrated assessment, with transparency, student engagement and guidelines to maintain standards (not tested). | Embed evaluative components, such as judging machine-generated content, into revised assessments (not tested). | Design and frame new prompts to centre the process of learning, higher-order thinking and authenticity, so that students see value in them (not tested).
limitations: Non-random voluntary convenience samples that likely over-represent interested respondents; snapshot from spring 2023; variation in disciplines; language issues for Greek-speaking Cypriot participants; no causal inference (Sec 5.3, p. 9). GPT-4 was used to help build codebooks for some open-ended data.
quality_note: Clear RQs; survey built on an established framework (Huber et al.); samples and context described in detail (Table 2); results supported by statistics and coded responses; limitations stated explicitly.
dim_authenticity: Authenticity was one rated dimension; respondents saw it falling with GenAI and recovering with adapted prompts.
dim_integrity_security: Seven-day take-home essays and coding tasks were seen as most exposed; academic integrity was rated the most important dimension by educators.
dim_lo_alignment: Authors argue assessment should shift towards evaluation and higher-order thinking, consistent with Bloom's revised taxonomy.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Tested prompts that build ChatGPT use into the task (critique/edit the essay; evaluate generated code and complexity analysis).
dim_accessibility_equity: Equity of access was one rated dimension; Cypriot students had much lower awareness of ChatGPT (42%).

title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
authors: Matt Bower; Jodie Torrington; Jennifer W. M. Lai; Peter Petocz; Mark Alfano
ft_reason: Most respondents are university teachers (222/318); how assessment should change under GenAI is a primary research question; peer-reviewed 2024 journal article.
study_design: Mixed-methods survey: general linear models on Likert impact ratings; inductive thematic analysis and UTAUT2-coded motivations with inter-rater reliability
country: International (Macquarie University, Australia-led; respondents from the Americas, Australasia, Europe, other)
discipline: Mixed (Arts & Humanities 71, Life Sciences 14, Physical Sciences 40, Social Sciences 129, Technology 59)
level: Mixed: 222 university, 82 high school, 14 primary teachers
sample: 318 educators (from 763 responses), collected 24 Jan-9 Mar 2023
assessment_types: Oral assessments; Supervised assessment; Process evidence; Personalised tasks; Staged submissions
key_findings: 61% of respondents rated GenAI's impact on assessment as major (38%) or profound (23%); only 7% said none. [pp. 15416-15417 / Sec 4.2.1 / Fig 2] | Greater awareness of GenAI predicted higher perceived impact (an 'ignorance effect'); gender, region and teaching level also influenced perceived impact. [p. 15417 / Sec 4.2.1; Sec 5.1] | Suggested assessment changes: higher-order thinking (n=71), more supervision/invigilation (n=69), authentic tasks (n=65), process focus (n=50), personalised tasks (n=35), spoken tasks such as mini-vivas (n=29), exams (n=21). [p. 15418 / Sec 4.2.2] | 54 respondents proposed embedding AI in assessment, e.g., students drafting with ChatGPT and then showing how they improved the draft. [p. 15418 / Sec 4.2.2] | Over 70% of motivations to change assessment were performance expectancy, mainly for students; authors stress the suggestions are perceptions, not evidence of efficacy. [pp. 15418-15419 / Sec 4.2.3; p. 15421 / Sec 5.3]
author_recommendations: Provide teacher professional learning on AI for assessment, built around performance-expectancy motivations (not tested) | Shift assessment toward in-person/invigilated, authentic, personalised, higher-order tasks with source disclosure (teacher perceptions, not tested) | Research the efficacy of teacher-proposed GenAI design patterns (not tested)
limitations: Self-selected social-media sample, not representative; small subgroup sizes; exploratory results; suggestions are perceptions only; early-2023 data (GPT-3.5).
quality_note: Rigorous mixed methods with reported kappa; HE not isolated in all analyses.
dim_authenticity: Authentic tasks were the third most frequent suggested assessment change (n=65).
dim_capability_verification: Spoken tasks/mini-vivas and invigilated exams proposed to confirm students' own work.
dim_integrity_security: Teachers' proposed changes were driven by plagiarism/unauthorised AI-use concerns, with a widespread call for more supervision.
dim_lo_alignment: Higher-order and critical thinking emphasised in redesigned assessment content.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Some teachers proposed integrating AI into tasks, with students showing how they enhanced AI drafts.
dim_workload: Some teachers expected AI to make assessment and feedback more efficient (effort expectancy n=15).
dim_process_visibility: Process-focused assessment (drafting, research booklets) suggested by 50 respondents.
dim_accessibility_equity: Literature review notes unequal access to AI may widen gaps for disadvantaged groups; not a survey finding.

title: Generative AI tools and assessment: Guidelines of the world's top-ranking universities
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse; Marie Alina Yeo; Yuwei Wan
ft_reason: Review of HE institutional guidance on GenAI in assessment design and academic integrity; peer-reviewed; 2023; English. The authors also conceptualise GAI assessment literacy.
study_design: Document review of public institutional guidelines (rapid systematic web review) with inductive coding and descriptive statistics
country: Hong Kong / Singapore (authors); guidelines from USA (15), UK (4), Canada (2), Japan (1), Australia (1)
sample: Top 50 universities in THE World University Rankings 2023; 30 had GAI guidance; 23 university-level instructor guidelines included after criteria; extracted 15 June 2023
assessment_types: Supervised assessment; Unsupervised formats; Oral assessments; Staged submissions; Process evidence; Personalised tasks; AI-use declarations
key_findings: Guidelines covered three areas: academic integrity (plagiarism, acknowledgement of GAI, detection), advice on assessment design, and communication with students (87% advised on communication). [Sec 2.3.2 p.4-5; Fig 1; Sec 3.3 p.7] | 57% of universities gave guidance on acknowledging or citing GAI use, with no standard approach. 61% mentioned detection tools, and most discouraged relying on them due to inaccuracy, privacy and trust concerns. [Sec 3.1.2-3.1.3 pp.5-6; Table 4] | 74% (17) gave assessment-design advice in five themes: test tasks on GAI, redesign tasks (creativity, context, authenticity, multimodal), focus on process and staged design (13 of 17), incorporate GAI into assessment, and use in-class assessment. [Sec 3.2 pp.6-7; Table 5] | Some guidelines cautioned that over-reliance on in-class or oral assessments limits what students can demonstrate and may disadvantage non-native speakers and students with disabilities. [Sec 3.2.5 p.7] | Authors propose 'GAI assessment literacy' for instructors: recognising integrity implications, designing tasks that incorporate GAI while evidencing learning, and communicating responsible use. [Sec 4 pp.8-9; Table 7]
author_recommendations: Institutions should develop, publish and regularly review GAI assessment guidelines (not tested) | Instructors should run assessment tasks through GAI to check how far it can complete them (not tested) | Have students use GAI as part of the assessment process and consider assessing GAI use in rubrics (not tested) | Develop instructors' GAI assessment literacy (preliminary conceptualisation, Table 7; not tested) | Adopt trust-based assessment practices and rational conversations with students about GAI implications (not tested)
limitations: Authors note: only publicly available guidelines; top-50 THE sample skews to the Global North and English-speaking institutions; only instructor-facing, university-level guidelines (p.9). Also a snapshot at June 2023, and counts differ between methods (30 found, 60%) and abstract/discussion (23, 'just under half').
quality_note: Transparent sampling frame, date and inclusion criteria; dual independent coding. The source is guidance documents, not evidence of effectiveness.
dim_authenticity: Argues that allowing GAI at stages of assessment would enhance authenticity, since GAI use will be ubiquitous in work.
dim_capability_verification: Reports one guideline (UCL) recommending an investigatory viva to probe authorship when AI use is suspected.
dim_integrity_security: Most guidelines discourage reliance on AI detectors; plagiarism definitions extended to AI-generated text and inadequate documentation.
dim_lo_alignment: Notes that GAI use can mean students demonstrate prompting skills rather than the targeted sub-skills, threatening validity.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Guidelines advise clear syllabus statements and open discussion of permissible use; authors argue for embracing GAI in assessment.
dim_scalability: Notes in-class assessment strategies may not be feasible for all classes.
dim_workload: Some guidelines advise balanced student workloads and longer deadlines, since time pressure is linked to improper GAI use.
dim_feasibility: Notes guidelines were developed rapidly and their suggestions are largely untested in practice.
dim_process_visibility: Guidelines recommend submitting notes, proposals, drafts, annotations and step lists, and breaking assignments into smaller pieces.
dim_accessibility_equity: Reports cautions that in-class or oral formats may disadvantage non-native English speakers and students needing accommodations; unequal tool access affects fairness.

title: The impact of generative AI on academic integrity of authentic assessments within a higher education context
authors: Alexander Kofinas; Crystal Han‐Huei Tsay; David Pike
ft_reason: Two UK universities (undergraduate business programmes); academic integrity of authentic assessments and GenAI detection in marking is the primary focus; GenAI (ChatGPT 3.5); peer-reviewed BJET article; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Exploratory two-phase within-subjects experiment (blind marking of human-authored, GenAI-modified and GenAI-generated scripts, then pair reconciliation) with descriptive statistics, followed by semi-structured interviews analysed thematically (mixed methods)
discipline: Business studies (BSc Business Management; BA Business Purchasing and Supply Chain Management)
sample: 8 academic markers in 4 pairs (3-15 years HE experience); per institution 21 writing samples (three levels, each with 3 original student scripts at three grade bands, 3 GenAI-modified versions and 1 GenAI-generated script); six assessments mapped for authenticity using Hobbins et al. (2022) and Kaider et al. (2017); four interviews of about 2 hours
key_findings: Pairs' accuracy in identifying which scripts involved GenAI ranged from 33.3% (7 of 21) to 85.7% (18 of 21); the most accurate pair included the module leader, who relied on familiarity with students' writing styles. [Results (RQ1), Tables 4-5, p. 2534-2536] | Markers' suspicion produced six false positives on original student work and seven false negatives on GenAI-modified or GenAI-generated work. [Results, Tables 4-5, p. 2536] | GenAI modification raised marks mainly in the 50-59 band (9 of 12 cases, by 2-8 points), while originally first-class scripts were often marked down, suggesting markers penalised work they saw as too perfect. [Results (RQ2), Tables 6-7, p. 2536-2539] | Six GenAI-generated scripts, each produced in 90 minutes or less by researchers acting as a 'mischievous' student, received upper-second marks (55-70). [Results, p. 2539] | Differences in assessment authenticity made very little difference to detecting GenAI use, so the authors conclude that authentic assessment alone is not a safeguard. [Discussion (RQ3), p. 2540]
author_recommendations: Give more critical attention to assessment design rather than relying on authenticity alone (not tested). | Shift towards performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments such as interactive orals and role-plays (not tested). | Assess process and socially situated knowledge application rather than written outputs (not tested). | Use GenAI intentionally in assessment design, for example to simulate professional scenarios (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge the experiment was exploratory with a small sample (Conclusions), and that markers' detection cues (e.g. disjointedness due to ChatGPT 3.5 limits) may not hold for newer models (Discussion). Also noted: convenience sampling at the authors' own institutions; markers knew some scripts involved GenAI, which may have biased marking; no third marker; descriptive statistics only; the RQ3 conclusion is not broken down by authenticity level in the tables.
quality_note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear RQs, appropriate exploratory design and well-described sample and materials. q4 Unclear because conclusions (especially RQ3 on authenticity) rest on descriptive counts from 8 markers without a per-authenticity analysis. Limitations are acknowledged only briefly.
dim_authenticity: Assessments ranging from low to moderate/high authenticity were all easily reproduced or modified with GenAI; more authentic tasks are also more complex and time-consuming to run (Methodology, Tables 1-2; Discussion).
dim_capability_verification: Argues that written, asynchronous outputs are no longer reliable indicators of learning and that performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments are needed (Conclusions).
dim_integrity_security: Markers could not reliably detect GenAI input, and suspicion led to both false positives and false negatives (Results, Tables 4-5).
dim_lo_alignment: Discusses constructive alignment and backwash as the basis for assessment design (Literature review).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Suggests GenAI could be used intentionally in assessment, for example to simulate professional environments or give iterative feedback (not tested) (Conclusions).
dim_scalability: Notes that highly authentic assessments are harder to manage with high student volumes (Discussion).
dim_workload: Notes that guidance requiring orals for every high AI-detection score would make marking far more onerous (Discussion).
dim_process_visibility: Recommends shifting from assessing outputs to assessing process and workplace relevance (Practitioner notes; Conclusions).
dim_accessibility_equity: Honest students may be penalised on suspicion alone, which raises a fairness concern (Results).

title: Comparison of generative AI performance on undergraduate and postgraduate written assessments in the biomedical sciences
authors: Andrew Evan Williams
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
ft_reason: UK HE (FHEQ levels 4-7); tests how vulnerable written essay assessments are to GenAI and what that means for assessment validity and integrity, which is a substantial focus; GenAI; peer-reviewed; 2024, English.

[Tables 2-5, pp. 6-13; Fig. 1, p. 16] | The tools did not perform better or worse in any noticeable way as FHEQ level rose. All three did relatively well at level 7, possibly reflecting the mechanistic topic of that question. [pp. 15, 19] | No tool supplied appropriate scientific references. Bing produced fully fabricated, realistically formatted references, and Bard misreported its word count. [pp. 17-18; Table 6] | Weaknesses across tools were mechanistic detail, specific examples from the literature, and critical insight. Coherence and scientific accuracy were generally strong for ChatGPT. author_recommendations: Train students in appropriate use of generative AI and its limitations, within institutional academic integrity policies (not tested) | Teachers may supervise or guide students' use of GenAI tools to ensure accuracy (not tested) | Future research should compare AI and student scripts blind, cover other assessment types (short answer, MCQ), and examine AI in assessment design and grading

dim_integrity_security: The author frames the findings as having implications for the design, implementation and grading of written assessments and for academic integrity (abstract; Conclusion p. 20).
dim_lo_alignment: AI output was benchmarked against FHEQ level descriptors and marking criteria mapped to them (pp. 4-5; Table 1).
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Recommends training students on the strengths and limits of LLMs, in the context of institutional integrity policies (pp. 19-20).

title: ChatGPT versus human essayists: an exploration of the impact of artificial intelligence for authorship and academic integrity in the humanities
authors: T. Revell; Will Yeadon; Glenn Cahilly-Bretzin; I. Clarke; G. Manning; J. Jones; Corinne Mulley; R. J. Pascual; N. Bradley; D. Thomas; Francis Leneghan
ft_reason: HE (first-year English undergraduates, Oxford); academic integrity, detectability and assessment design are primary; GenAI (GPT-4); peer reviewed; 2024. Non-computing discipline.
study_design: Blinded comparative marking study plus AI-detector evaluation, with qualitative analysis of marker comments

dim_lo_alignment: Argues output-based mean-score grading is no longer a valid proxy for computational-thinking outcomes.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: Recommends staged AI permission, from No-AI foundations to AI-assisted projects to manual validation of AI code (not tested).

key_findings: Students diagnose and repair a deliberately flawed professional pitch, which makes reasoning visible and is reported to reduce template-driven answers. [Abstract; closing appraisal section]
author_recommendations: Use deliberately broken cases with bounded GenAI use and graded usage declarations.
limitations: Needs careful scaffolding and subtle errors, and was not formally evaluated.
redesign_note: Describes a specific GenAI-aware assessment design with a graded AI-use declaration.
quality_note: Practice description without formal evaluation.
dim_authenticity: Uses professionally presented pitches with realistic flaws.
dim_appropriate_ai_use: GenAI permitted only for ideation and visualisation during redesign, with a structured usage declaration in the rubric.
dim_scalability: Authors state it scales across large cohorts.
